---
title: "Limitations"
description: "When the OPDI data are missing or wrong: limits that apply to the whole dataset, and a summary of the limits of each method with links to the details."
---

This page says where the OPDI data should not be trusted, or should be used
with care. The first part covers limits that apply to the whole dataset. The
second part gives one short summary per method, with a link to the full list
on its methods page.

## Limits of the whole dataset

### ADS-B reception {#ads-b-reception}

Everything in OPDI comes from **ADS-B** (Automatic Dependent
Surveillance–Broadcast) messages: radio messages in which an aircraft
broadcasts its position, altitude and speed. They are heard only by a
receiver within radio range, which is a few hundred kilometres at cruise
altitude and much less near the ground. The OpenSky Network's receivers are
run by volunteers and institutions, and they are not spread evenly.

- Where no receiver is near, there are no data. This is often the case over
  the oceans, over large areas with few receivers, and on the ground at many
  airports.
- An event that needs reception on the ground (block times, runway events,
  airport surface events) is missing wherever the airport surface is not
  heard. Its absence does not mean that the event did not happen.
- Aircraft without ADS-B, or that do not broadcast it, are not in the data.
- Counts made from OPDI (flights per airport, movements per runway) are
  therefore lower bounds, not totals. How much of an airport's traffic OPDI
  sees varies from one airport to another and from one day to the next: see
  [OPDI Sensors: where next](../sensors-expansion.qmd) for a measurement over
  European airports in 2025.

### No flight plan data

OPDI uses no flight plans. A **flight** in OPDI is a **track**: the position
reports of one aircraft that belong together (see
[Track identity](../methods/track-identity.qmd)). It starts where reception
starts and ends where reception ends.

- The departure and destination airports are found from the track. They are
  empty when the track begins or ends away from an airport (see
  [Departure and destination airports](../methods/airports.qmd)).
- Nothing about the planned route, the planned times or the airline schedule
  is known. Delays against a schedule cannot be computed from OPDI alone.
- A flight that is split into two tracks gives two rows in the flight list.

### Day of a flight

A flight belongs to the day on which it was first seen, in UTC, and all its
events are in the files of that day (see
[Data](index.qmd#which-day-a-flight-belongs-to)). As a result:

- The events of one file can happen on the next day.
- To count the events or landings that **happened** on one day, read that
  day's files and the files of the day before, and filter on `event_time`.
- A flight first seen just before midnight UTC belongs to the earlier day,
  even if it took off after midnight.

### One AIRAC cycle for the airspace

The flight information regions used for `xing-fir` are those of one AIRAC
cycle, 524 (valid 2024-11-28 to 2024-12-26), for every day. An **AIRAC
cycle** is the 28-day period in which changes to aeronautical data such as
airspace boundaries take effect. Where a boundary has moved since that cycle,
the crossings follow the old boundary. See
[FIR crossings](../methods/fir-crossings.qmd#limitations).

### Accuracy measured on European airports

Most methods were checked against EUROCONTROL Network Manager data, which
cover flights in the European area. The airports used for the checks are
mostly those with the best reception. Elsewhere in the world, and at airports
with less reception, the accuracy has not been measured and is likely to be
lower. Several items have not been compared with any reference at all: the
[Validation summary](../methods/validation-summary.qmd) marks them "Not
validated".

### Open reference data

Airports and runways come from OurAirports, airport layouts and stand names
from OpenStreetMap, and aircraft details from the OpenSky aircraft database.
An error or a gap in these open sources carries over into OPDI: a runway
missing from OurAirports gives no runway events, and an unmapped stand gives
no block time.

## Limits of each method

### Track identity

A track can hold reception gaps of up to 10 hours; never interpolate across a
silence of more than 30 minutes. A flight can still be split into several
tracks, and, rarely, two flights of one aircraft can be joined. `flight_id`
values of different releases do not match.
[All limitations](../methods/track-identity.qmd#limitations).

### Trajectory cleaning

Cleaning empties values that cannot be trusted; it does not repair them, so
many positions, altitudes and speeds are missing. Jamming of satellite
navigation is not removed.
[All limitations](../methods/trajectory-cleaning.qmd#limitations).

### Departure and destination airports

About one departure in five and one arrival in three get no airport. Small
airfields and heliports are never named. The method was checked in the
European area only.
[All limitations](../methods/airports.qmd#limitations).

### Take-off and landing

The published take-off and landing times mix two methods with different
shifts; the field `method` in `info` tells them apart. Most reference times
are rounded to the minute, so differences under about 30 s could only be
judged at three airports. A track keeps at most one take-off and one landing.
[All limitations](../methods/takeoff-landing.qmd#limitations).

### Block times

Off-block times tend to be late and in-block times early, by about a minute,
so taxi times computed from them are too short. The events need reception at
the stand and stands mapped in OpenStreetMap.
[All limitations](../methods/block-times.qmd#limitations).

### Runway milestones

Line-up, runway vacated, runway crossings and go-arounds have not been
compared with reference data. They need reception on the runway, and their
times can be off by up to 5 s.
[All limitations](../methods/runway-milestones.qmd#limitations).

### Airport surface events

Not compared with reference data. The events depend on ground reception and
on OpenStreetMap; areas overlap, so one movement can give several events at
the same time, and passing over a stand is not parking there.
[All limitations](../methods/surface-events.qmd#limitations).

### Vertical events

Not compared with reference data. `level-start` and `level-end` fit
turboprops and light aircraft poorly; for vertical efficiency indicators, use
the level-offs. A track that starts in the air can have its top of climb at
its first position.
[All limitations](../methods/vertical-events.qmd#limitations).

### Distance rings

Only arrival crossings of the 40 NM and 100 NM rings were checked. Rings are
drawn only around the airports the flight list names, so a wrong airport gives
crossings around the wrong airport.
[All limitations](../methods/distance-rings.qmd#limitations).

### Holding

Checked on one day at two airports in Western Europe. Short holds, and holds
flown low or slowly, are not reported.
[All limitations](../methods/holding.qmd#limitations).

### Point merge

Checked by eye at one airport on one day. Only the airports in OPDI's table of
merge points are examined.
[All limitations](../methods/point-merge.qmd#limitations).

### FIR crossings

Compared with the exact boundaries of the regions, not with Network Manager
records. One AIRAC cycle is used for every day, and a visit of less than
60 seconds gives no crossing.
[All limitations](../methods/fir-crossings.qmd#limitations).

### Measurements

The distance flown follows the received positions and a straight line across
gaps, so it is shorter than the path really flown. Both measurements count
from the start of the track, not from off-block or take-off.
[All limitations](../methods/measurements.qmd#limitations).

### First seen and last seen

These are the first and last position received, not the off-block and
in-block times. The position of the last report is often a few minutes old.
[All limitations](../methods/first-last-seen.qmd#limitations).
